contexts.text: A 52‑year‑old woman who works in sugarcane fields in a rural area was referred to Oral Medicine for evaluation of a granulomatous lesion on the palate and for hoarseness that she thought followed a flu 3 months earlier. According to the referring surgeon, she had an extensive oral lesion and had undergone laryngoscopy and biopsy; that biopsy produced a histopathological result of “pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia and an active chronic inflammatory process, suggesting a fungus investigation,” prompting the referral. She reported no chronic systemic disease or regular medications. She described a history of crusting and nasal bleeding that began about 4 years earlier. On examination she had nasal obstruction, a nasal (hyponasal) voice, and was a mouth breather. She had smoked for 6 months and used both upper and lower complete dental prostheses continuously. Extrabuccal exam showed a lowering of the right nasal wing and a nasal septum perforation. Intrabuccal exam revealed a granulomatous lesion involving the entire palate and uvula, extending bilaterally to the pharynx with an erythematous appearance and areas of scratchable white plaques.

A 30-year-old Caucasian man, unemployed, HIV-negative and with no other concomitant infections, presented in 2014 with a papule on the inferior eyelid of the right eye. His past history included, in 2008, an isolated nodulation in the right leg that resolved after treatment. Over time new lesions progressively appeared on the chest, abdomen, back, feet, and in the oral cavity. Ulcerated oral lesions were present on the hard palate and on the left and right jugal mucosa. Disease progression was associated with fever, headache, and weight loss.

A 38‑year‑old man from Yayu district, western Ethiopia, presented to the outpatient clinic with multiple skin lesions on his face and hands and mutilation of the nose; his upper lip was injured and swollen. Eight years earlier he had a small papule on the right cheek that progressed to an open ulcer, then to ulcers on the left cheek and forehead; those active lesions lasted about six months and healed spontaneously, leaving permanent hypopigmented scars. He had no fever, hepatosplenomegaly or lymphedema and reported no history of HIV, chronic disease, alcohol abuse, or immunomodulatory drug use. Parasitological testing of lesion smears at that time showed many macrophages filled with amastigote stages of Leishmania, graded as +6. A nonreactive rK39 rapid diagnostic test and absence of related systemic signs made visceral leishmaniasis unlikely. Based on the clinical manifestations and smear result he was diagnosed with mucocutaneous leishmaniasis and treated with intramuscular sodium stibogluconate (20 mg/kg/day for 30 days) with clinical cure. Two years later he returned with a different cutaneous eruption that had appeared over the previous three months and had been preceded by intense itching. On exam he had multiple, nonpitting, closed papules on his face, nose, hands and legs. A skin smear again showed intramacrophage amastigotes with a parasite load graded +6, and culture grew promastigotes.

A 9-year-old boy presented with multiple papular lesions on the left cheek that had been present for three months and had gradually enlarged. His medical history was notable for an episode of cutaneous leishmaniasis located on the nose two years earlier, which had completely regressed after treatment with intralesional meglumine antimonate. Dermatologic examination showed multiple, coalescing, rough, slightly elevated, yellowish-brown papular lesions 3–6 mm in diameter on the left cheek. He also had a large atrophic scar on the nose. Nothing of interest was noted in his family history or his laboratory tests.

A 61-year-old man (weight 65 kg) was referred in January with a 2-month history of a 1 × 3 cm lesion on the left ear. He has diabetes and had not traveled outside Kashan during the previous year. He reported that the ear lesion felt uncomfortable and scabrous but was not painful and he had no systemic complaints. Direct microscopy of scales with 10% potassium hydroxide (KOH) preparation was negative for fungal elements. The lesion was cleaned and specimens were collected from the margin by scraping; two smears were fixed with methanol and stained with 10% Giemsa for 30 minutes. On microscopic examination of the stained smears, amastigote forms of Leishmania spp. were observed.

A 74-year-old woman from Tunis presented with several weeks of fever (oral temperature 38–39°C), sweats, chills, fatigue, diarrhea, intermittent vague abdominal pain, and occasional dry cough. Her only medical history was well-controlled hypertension. Examination showed a palpable spleen just below the left costal margin. The rest of the exam was essentially normal. Renal, liver, and coagulation tests were normal. A Leishmania rk39 immunochromatography test was positive. Bone marrow aspiration parasitology revealed Leishmania amastigote forms, and serum immunofluorescence for Leishmania antibodies was positive (titer 1:400). Blood qPCR detected Leishmania DNA (400 parasites/mL). Direct microscopy of skin smears from the arm lesion showed no amastigotes, but Leishmania DNA amplification was obtained from dermal DNA extract by qPCR. ITS1 sequencing showed the Leishmania strains from the blood and the arm lesion corresponded to L. infantum and were 100% identical. Systemic response was rapid: fever resolved, general condition improved, splenomegaly regressed, blood counts normalized, and blood qPCR became negative after 28 days. However, "the skin lesion did not improve although Leishmania qPCR on dermal sample became negative." A skin biopsy was initially refused. One year later the lesion remained essentially unchanged. A polarized dermoscopy examination showed "ulcerations and short, fine arborizing vessels," described as evocative of a basal cell carcinoma.

A 52-year-old male farm worker from Ceara state, northeast Brazil, presented with a 4-month history of skin lesions. Lesions appeared first on the face and legs, than spread across much of his body, including the genitalia, soles of feet, and scalp. He reported daily fevers for the first 2 weeks of illness. On examination the patient had 178 lesions of different sizes and aspects; ulcerated, crusted, papular, nodular, and pustular. Many had apparent bacterial superinfections. The remainder of the physical examination was normal. A complete blood count and liver and kidney function tests were within normal limits. Serological tests for syphilis and human immunodeficiency virus were negative.

A 41-year-old Caucasian man was admitted during treatment with intravenous liposomal amphotericin B for laryngeal and facial mucocutaneous leishmaniasis because of marked elevation of creatine kinase (CK) (more than 10× upper limit of normal during admission; pretreatment CK up to ~2× ULN previously) and rising serum creatinine. Past medical history was notable for visceral leishmaniasis at age 13, recurrent otitis and an episode of bronchopneumonia in childhood, long-standing unexplained elevated CK attributed in the past to occupation and boxing, and chronic periorbital/facial swelling first noted in 2013. In January 2019 he developed hoarseness and dysphonia; laryngoscopy and biopsy were positive for Leishmania spp., and earlier periocular skin samples (2015) were retrospectively PCR-positive for Leishmania spp. He reported no travel outside Europe. There was a family history notable for a brother who died at age 20 from an unspecified lymphoproliferative disease and a sister with chronic myalgias. On examination he was in good general condition with bilateral orbital swelling. Peripheral blood count was unremarkable. B-cell immunophenotyping disclosed a defect in the memory compartment with markedly low switched-memory B cells. There was no history of liver or biliary tract disease or neutropenia. The patient met criteria for common-variable immunodeficiency, but because of the opportunistic, persistent Leishmania infection further genetic studies were pursued.

A 55-year-old man from the Manaus region with no comorbidities had been treated for cutaneous leishmaniasis. He had completed treatment with a pentavalent antimonial drug 40 days earlier and had received a second outpatient 30-day cycle; ten days after the end of that treatment his leishmaniasis lesion was healed. He then developed grouped microvesicles on an erythematous-infiltrated base that began in the neck and ascended toward the right scalp margin. The vesicles involved the right pinna, external auditory canal, and right ear lobe and were associated with severe torticollis-like pain along the nerve distribution. HIV serology was negative.

A 53-year-old man from Mundo Novo, State of Bahia, Brazil, presented in July with pain, nasal obstruction, odynophagia, and dysphagia. On examination there was a painful, hyperemic, friable lesion in the right nasal cavity and an infiltrative lesion involving the hard palate, soft palate, and uvula. Additional findings included an ulcerated lesion on the left eyebrow and right eye with seropurulent secretion, a small ulcer on the lower eyelid, a lesion on the lobe of the right ear, and a lesion in the malar region. The patient was admitted for diagnosis and management of disseminated skin lesions. A biopsy of the palate lesions showed a non-specific erosive chronic inflammatory process. HIV testing was negative.

*   **Reference Case Support:** Context 2 describes a patient presenting with mucocutaneous leishmaniasis following prior cutaneous lesions, fitting the clinical trajectory.

*   **Infectious/Inflammatory Pseudotumor (Non-Leishmaniasis):** Chronic granulomatous infections (e.g., fungal infections, tuberculosis) can cause extensive mucosal thickening and papillomatous lesions in the oropharynx, mimicking MCL. *   **Squamous Cell Carcinoma (SCC):** Chronic inflammation and mucosal lesions in the oropharynx can mimic parasitic infections. Context 3 notes that a persistent lesion resembling MCL could eventually be mistaken for a basal cell carcinoma, highlighting the need to differentiate malignancy from chronic infection.
*   **Other Mucosal Infections:** Severe fungal infections or viral etiologies must be considered given the severe mucosal involvement.

Eight years earlier he had a small papule on the right cheek that progressed to an open ulcer, then to ulcers on the left cheek and forehead; those active lesions lasted about six months and healed spontaneously, leaving permanent hypopigmented scars. Two years later he returned with a different cutaneous eruption that had appeared over the previous three months and had been preceded by intense itching. On exam he had multiple, nonpitting, closed papules on his face, nose, hands and legs. A skin smear again showed intramacrophage amastigotes with a parasite load graded +6, and culture grew promastigotes.

A 38‑year‑old man from Yayu district, western Ethiopia, presented to the outpatient clinic with multiple skin lesions on his face and hands and mutilation of the nose; his upper lip was injured and swollen. Eight years earlier he had a small papule on the right cheek that progressed to an open ulcer, then to ulcers on the left cheek and forehead; those active lesions lasted about six months and healed spontaneously, leaving permanent hypopigmented scars. He had no fever, hepatosplenomegaly or lymphedema and reported no history of HIV, chronic disease, alcohol abuse, or immunomodulatory drug use. Parasitological testing of lesion smears at that time showed many macrophages filled with amastigote stages of Leishmania, graded as +6. A nonreactive rK39 rapid diagnostic test and absence of related systemic signs made visceral leishmaniasis unlikely. Based on the clinical manifestations and smear result he was diagnosed with mucocutaneous leishmaniasis and treated with intramuscular sodium stibogluconate (20 mg/kg/day for 30 days) with clinical cure. Two years later he returned with a different cutaneous eruption that had appeared over the previous three months and had been preceded by intense itching. On exam he had multiple, nonpitting, closed papules on his face, nose, hands and legs. A skin smear again showed intramacrophage amastigotes with a parasite load graded +6, and culture grew promastigotes.

An 84‑year‑old woman presented with a large nodular lesion on the forehead of 2.5 months' duration. She had been seen at another hospital where a pre‑diagnosis of lymphoma was recorded; the prior punch biopsy report listed basal cell carcinoma, sarcoidosis, lupus vulgaris and pseudolymphoma among the clinical pre‑diagnoses and the material was sent for pathology consultation. Microscopic examination of the punch biopsy showed a dense nodular and diffuse lymphohistiocytic cell infiltration within the dermis. In the cytoplasm of histiocytes, small, round structures resembling organisms were noted. Immunohistochemical staining showed reactive T lymphocytes labelled with CD3 and CD5, reactive B lymphocytes labelled with CD20, and large clusters of histiocytes labelled with CD68; there was no staining with CD30. The pathology report recommended investigation of the aetiology of granulomatous dermatitis, especially cutaneous leishmaniasis.

She initially noted a papule in the left malar region that later ulcerated and increased in size. Fifteen days after the facial lesion appeared, she developed another lesion on the right knee.

Her only medical history was well-controlled hypertension. Examination showed a palpable spleen just below the left costal margin. On the right arm near the axilla there was "a single well-defined, ulcer surrounded by erythematous edging, with serous oozing" about 3 × 3 cm; the patient reported the lesion was painless, nonhealing, and present for 2–3 years. The rest of the exam was essentially normal. A Leishmania rk39 immunochromatography test was positive. Bone marrow aspiration parasitology revealed Leishmania amastigote forms, and serum immunofluorescence for Leishmania antibodies was positive (titer 1:400). Blood qPCR detected Leishmania DNA (400 parasites/mL). Direct microscopy of skin smears from the arm lesion showed no amastigotes, but Leishmania DNA amplification was obtained from dermal DNA extract by qPCR. ITS1 sequencing showed the Leishmania strains from the blood and the arm lesion corresponded to L. infantum and were 100% identical. Systemic response was rapid: fever resolved, general condition improved, splenomegaly regressed, blood counts normalized, and blood qPCR became negative after 28 days. However, "the skin lesion did not improve although Leishmania qPCR on dermal sample became negative." A skin biopsy was initially refused. One year later the lesion remained essentially unchanged. A polarized dermoscopy examination showed "ulcerations and short, fine arborizing vessels," described as evocative of a basal cell carcinoma.

A 78-year-old man from a rural area in western Iran was referred for multiple ulcerative, exudative lesions involving the mid-face (upper lip and anterior nasal fossa), above the eyebrows, dorsal aspects of both hands, and posterior aspects of both heels. Lesions began three years earlier as papules on the dorsal hands and progressively enlarged to involve the face and heels and became ulcerative; involvement of the right hand progressed to destruction of tendons and soft tissue of the fifth finger, resulting in amputation of that finger. He had no history of comorbid conditions, no regular medications reported, and denied systemic symptoms — there was no weight loss, fever, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly or other signs of systemic involvement on examination or routine laboratory survey. Multiple prior empirical treatments for different presumed diagnoses, including pyoderma gangrenosum, sarcoidosis, and leishmaniasis, had been tried without improvement. An initial skin biopsy showed a necrotizing and palisading granulomatous tissue pattern that suggested an infectious etiology, but initial smears of lesion material for fungal elements, mycobacteria and Leishmania were negative. A tuberculin skin test produced a 27 mm induration, and anti-tuberculosis therapy (isoniazid, rifampin, ethambutol, and pyrazinamide) was started.

A 52-year-old male farm worker from Ceara state, northeast Brazil, presented with a 4-month history of skin lesions. Lesions appeared first on the face and legs, than spread across much of his body, including the genitalia, soles of feet, and scalp. He reported daily fevers for the first 2 weeks of illness. On examination the patient had 178 lesions of different sizes and aspects; ulcerated, crusted, papular, nodular, and pustular. Many had apparent bacterial superinfections. The remainder of the physical examination was normal. A complete blood count and liver and kidney function tests were within normal limits. Serological tests for syphilis and human immunodeficiency virus were negative.

A 55-year-old man from the Manaus region with no comorbidities had been treated for cutaneous leishmaniasis. He had completed treatment with a pentavalent antimonial drug 40 days earlier and had received a second outpatient 30-day cycle; ten days after the end of that treatment his leishmaniasis lesion was healed. He then developed grouped microvesicles on an erythematous-infiltrated base that began in the neck and ascended toward the right scalp margin. The vesicles involved the right pinna, external auditory canal, and right ear lobe and were associated with severe torticollis-like pain along the nerve distribution. HIV serology was negative.

A 22‑month‑old girl presented with 8 days of fever to 40°C and mild cough. Past history: failure to thrive; normal neurologic development. She was the first child of a non‑consanguineous couple; no family history of albinism; normal hair and skin. On exam she was stunted, pale, had non‑tender hepatomegaly 5–6 cm and splenomegaly palpable 4 cm below the left costal margin. Petechial rash developed on the chest and legs as she worsened. Initial laboratory results: WBC 5100/mm3 (ANC 1200/mm3), Hb 9.1 g/dl, platelets 47,000/mm3; mild transaminase elevation; hypoalbuminemia. Ferritin 1,134 ng/ml; soluble IL‑2 receptor (sCD25) 3,183 U/ml. Blood cultures were negative. Serum immunoglobulins and lymphocyte subsets were reported as normal. Infectious testing: EBV serology positive for IgM and IgG anti‑VCA with negative IgG anti‑EBNA; EBV viral load 637 copies/ml. Leishmania testing was discordant: immunochromatography and indirect immunofluorescence were negative, serum ELISA was slightly positive, and leishmanial antigen in urine was negative. Bone‑marrow aspiration revealed hemophagocytosis. Over the next day she clinically worsened with progressive splenomegaly and cytopenias (WBC 4,800/mm3 with ANC 800/mm3, Hb 6.8 g/dl, platelets 27,000/mm3), triglycerides 686 mg/dl, ferritin 3,849 ng/ml, and sCD25 3,596 U/ml. Clotting tests were normal and perforin expression by flow cytometry was reported as normal.
